chapters.title: A Spring Dream
chapters.content:
"Yan'er, does it feel good?"
Beneath the dim bed curtains, the hazy warmth filtering through the gauze veil left Xi Rongyan's gaze soft and unfocused.
Inside the warm canopy, a sweet, heady fragrance set her whole body aflame, and her body moved instinctively toward the tall, scorching figure before her.
She could hear her own breathing — shallow, unfamiliar — her fingers clutching tight at the man's white collar as her body ached with wanting.
Within the swirling, gauze-draped warmth, she could not make out the man's face.
Her vision blurred with tears as discomfort washed over her, and then a low, deep laugh sounded near her ear as he pulled her firmly into his arms.
His broad fingers traced along the corners of her eyes and brows, finally coming to rest on her damp back.
She glimpsed his deep, desire-laden eyes gazing at her, and then he whispered with a sigh: "Yan'er, we will have a child very soon."
"You will forget him before long."
"You can only be mine."
His scorching palms cradled her yielding body, filling her with an exquisite, aching pleasure.
—
When Xi Rongyan woke on her bed, she stared at the familiar curtains for a long while, dazed.
The scene from her dream had felt so real that it seemed to linger even now.
As though she were still inside that canopy, heavy with its hazy, intimate fragrance.
Only when the world around her gradually reasserted itself did she manage to sit up, propping herself upright.
Who was the man in her dream...
And those eyes — dangerous yet cold...
She touched her cheeks. They were warm. Her heart would not stop racing.
Her slender pale fingers pressed against her temple as her dark hair cascaded forward over her white underrobe. She let out a slow breath.
A thin sheen of sweat had gathered on her back.
She had been having these dreams night after night lately, yet she could never make out the man's face.
Beyond the bed curtains, a silk lantern brightened, and a maidservant's voice called from outside. Xi Rongyan murmured a soft reply, and only then was the curtain lifted.
A soft, warm yellow light poured in. Baozhu saw that Xi Rongyan's face — that lotus-bloom complexion — held a sheen of water in her eyes, a faint flush on her jade-white cheeks, and even her brow was touched with a fine, delicate sweat.
Several wisps of long hair clung to her damp cheeks, lending her an almost bewitching air. Baozhu was startled.
Outside, a light rain still fell. She quickly turned back to tell another maidservant to close the window that had been left open a crack, then looked at Xi Rongyan with concern. "Miss, have you caught a chill again?"
It was only the beginning of spring, and the air still carried a lingering bite. It had rained softly for two days now.
And in the days before, Miss had cried herself into sorrow over the matter of Young Master Gu — she had been melancholy ever since.
Perhaps she had not been careful and had caught a chill without realizing it.
But Xi Rongyan shook her head and murmured, "Just a dream."
She sat up on the edge of the bed, staring at the carpet below, her thoughts slipping away again for a moment.
She had even dreamed of being pressed to her knees on that very carpet by the man...
Xi Rongyan's face paled slightly, her cool fingers pressed over her flushed cheeks, and she felt at a loss.
She did not understand why she was having such dreams.
She had never even read those sorts of vulgar books, let alone ever seen a man's body.
How could it be like this?
Baozhu saw Xi Rongyan bow her head and cover her face, her hair slipping from her shoulders, and asked anxiously, "Miss, what is wrong?"
"Should I send for the physician?"
Xi Rongyan shook her head. Only once the last trace of warmth had faded from her cheeks did she say softly, "Help me dress first. We'll go see Mother."
Only then did Baozhu call Huashan to come help Xi Rongyan with her clothing.
As she sat at her dressing table, Xi Rongyan looked at her own reflection in the bronze mirror and seemed to see again the unfocused eyes she had worn in her dream.
She drew a deep breath and called for a maidservant to push open the window.
The cool breeze drifted in. She listened to the soft rustle of rain and watched the camellia outside swaying in the drizzle, and at last her heart grew a little calmer.
She would think no more of that dream.
Once dressed, she went to pay her respects to her mother.
Her mother had never been in robust health, and had fallen ill again these past two days. Xi Rongyan sat at the bedside, her heart aching a little, and said softly to her mother's wan face, "Mother will recover soon."
Lady Xie leaned against the soft pillows behind her, a cloth bound across her brow. Even in illness, the beautiful woman's colour held.
Worry showed in her eyes. She took Xi Rongyan's hand and sighed quietly, "Rongyan, my illness needs only a little more rest to mend. What I worry about now is you."
"After this affair, I fear those with ill intentions will spread unkind words about you outside."
Xi Rongyan knew what her mother was worried about. Gossip had already been circulating outside.
At times Xi Rongyan herself wondered whether she truly was, as people said, a blight upon her betrothed.
When Xi Rongyan was three, her father had arranged a childhood betrothal for her.
Her intended was Zhang Jingsheng, the eldest grandson of the greatly respected Grand Tutor Zhang.
But when Zhang Jingsheng was six, he had been playing near a pond and accidentally fallen in. By the time a servant discovered him and pulled him out, he had already drawn his last breath.
Though the incident was later traced back to strife among the master's wives and concubines, it nonetheless planted a seed that would haunt Xi Rongyan's reputation in the years to come.
Then, when Xi Rongyan was ten, another match was arranged.
It was to Gu Yunyu — the eldest legitimate son of the Gu family, a household of scholarly repute.
Xi Rongyan and Gu Yunyu could be said to have grown up together.
Her own father served as a Huangmen Shilang in the Chancellery; Gu Yunyu's father was in the Hanlin Academy. The two men had been close friends since their days at the Imperial Academy, and their families were of matched standing.
Her mother and Gu Yunyu's mother had once been intimate companions in their girlhood years, and the two households kept frequent company.
Young Master Gu Yunyu was handsome and refined, a man of cultured sensibilities. Two years prior he had passed the imperial examinations and been appointed as a Judge in the Capital Prefectural Court — a man of every promise.
More importantly, Gu Yunyu had always been attentive and considerate toward Xi Rongyan. Though he had never once overstepped propriety, she could feel his care in every small thing.
Xi Rongyan had looked forward to this union with genuine happiness in her heart.
Both families had already set the date — she need only wait for the wedding in the fifth month to become his wife.
Yet, who could have foreseen that half a month ago, while Gu Yunyu and several close friends from his examination cohort were enjoying a spring outing, they encountered brigands on the road. In the struggle, Gu Yunyu was struck in the chest with a dagger and fell to the ground.
He never woke again.
When Xi Rongyan heard the news she was overcome with grief, unable to believe it.
Only when she heard her father speak the words himself did she feel the searing pain of her heart being torn apart.
She dimly remembered the sachet Gu Yunyu had given her at the Qixi Festival, with its inscription of "a lifetime together," and felt as though her heart had been gouged out.
She could not make sense of it in those dark days — she had waited in such joyful anticipation to be married, so why had she been dealt this blow?
How could a man as good and gentle as Yunyu gege have met such a fate?
Those bandits had been caught and would answer with their lives, but who could restore the life of Yunyu gege?
Even now, recalling it brought tears to Xi Rongyan's eyes.
She looked at her mother and said hoarsely, "What people say outside is their affair — I do not care."
"Even if I never marry, so long as I can remain by Mother's side, I will be content."
Lady Xie gazed at her daughter's face and sighed again, softly: "How can you say such a thing?"
"The talk out there will follow you, and this business has already made it difficult to arrange another match."
"Since the Empress Dowager has summoned you to the palace for a visit, go and present yourself properly."
"If the Empress Dowager can arrange a suitable match for you, I will be at ease."

chapters.title: An Encounter with the Emperor
chapters.content:
Xi Rongyan lowered her gaze, her fingers tightening around the embroidered handkerchief she held. "Mother," she said softly, "Yunyu gege has only just passed, and the Empress Dowager is already arranging another match for me. What will people think?"
"They will say I am heartless and faithless."
As she spoke, Xi Rongyan closed her eyes briefly and murmured, "And besides, I am in no hurry to be betrothed."
Xi Rongyan's words were not without reason.
Lady Xie understood why her daughter spoke as she did.
Yet it was not she who was in a hurry — it was Xi Rongyan's age that would not wait.
Xi Rongyan had come of age last September, and her mother had hoped to move the wedding forward. But the auspicious date selected by the diviner was the fifth month of this very year. Now that Xi Rongyan was already past fifteen and a half, if the matter dragged on until she was sixteen, her age would begin to count against her.
Even if they became betrothed now, with all the formalities to be observed, the earliest she could be married was before year's end.
And if it took longer still, the wedding would not happen until next year.
Lady Xie patted her daughter's hand with a sigh. "Let us set this aside for now. The Empress Dowager has summoned you to the palace today — go and see her first, then we will speak further."
Xi Rongyan nodded, remained a little longer to keep her mother company, and then took her leave.
When she stepped out onto the covered corridor, the fine rain was still falling. The damp air settled over her, carrying a faint melancholy, and her thoughts returned to Gu Yunyu.
She thought of how good he had always been to her.
Then she thought of two days ago, when Gu Yunyu's younger sister had come running to her in tears, accusing her through her sobs of being the cause of her elder brother's death.
After a long pause, Xi Rongyan lowered her head, raised her umbrella, and stepped into the rain.
Her silver silk gauze skirt swept into the downpour, its hem flickering like a shadow across the wet bluestone path.
—
Xi Rongyan had visited the Empress Dowager's Cining Palace many times before.
The Empress Dowager was her father's elder sister. As a child, her father had always brought her, her sister, and her eldest brother to the palace to pay their respects.
In former days it had been Kuntai Palace; now it was Cining Palace.
By this time the drizzle had stopped, and the stone tiles of the walkway glistened with moisture.
She walked carefully along the long palace corridors. The rules of the palace were far stricter than outside, and she kept her composure, head slightly bowed, careful not to make even the smallest mistake.
Two court ladies passed nearby. She caught their sidelong glances and the sound of their whispered voices from the corner of her eye.
Involuntarily, she gripped her hands. Had the rumors outside already reached the palace?
Suddenly the head attendant leading the way came to a halt and turned to murmur to Xi Rongyan, "Fourth Young Miss, the Emperor is coming."
It was not the first time Xi Rongyan had encountered the Emperor during a palace visit. She kept her composure, observed propriety, and stopped alongside the head attendant to perform a palace courtesy as the Emperor's palanquin passed.
When the imperial procession approached, Xi Rongyan's heart tightened slightly with a tremor of anxiety.
She hoped it would pass quickly.
Her thoughts drifted back to the time two years ago when she had been visiting the palace and happened upon eunuchs carrying a figure wrapped in white cloth. The white cloth bore smears and blossoms of blood, and the pale fingertips left exposed were still trickling.
One of the eunuchs had recognized the head attendant from the Empress Dowager's palace and come over to pay his respects. The attendant had asked idly, and learned that beneath the white cloth lay a newly arrived beauty who had transgressed one of the Emperor's forbidden matters and had been beaten to death with wooden rods.
Those around had worn calm expressions, as though nothing more than an ordinary death had occurred.
The attendant beside her had merely nodded, as though it were the most unremarkable thing in the world.
Xi Rongyan had stood transfixed, staring at that bloodstained white cloth. She had nightmares afterward.
From that day on, she carried a trace of fear toward the Emperor.
She still could not fathom what manner of transgression would see a person beaten to death.
But the procession before her suddenly stopped. Xi Rongyan saw only a pair of black boots embroidered with golden dragons come to rest before her. Her fingers tensed around the handkerchief she held, and she quickly performed a half-kneeling salute. "This subject pays her respects to Your Majesty."
Wei Qi glanced downward at Xi Rongyan's slender fingers, clenched tight with anxiety. His gaze swept across the elegant slope of her nose, then settled on the jade-green earrings swaying at her cheeks.
Trembling with unease.
Wei Qi's eyes deepened. She was still this frightened of him.
He watched her long lashes flutter, just as they had in his former life — when she lay in his arms and always, restlessly, tried to pull away.
Seeing her again, that sensation of having recovered something lost sent his emotions taut, filling him with a fierce need to bind this woman to his side more tightly still.
His hand lifted of its own accord, wanting to touch her — but he had forgotten. At this moment, Xi Rongyan was still a sheltered, unmarried girl of good family.
The Empress Dowager would make another suitable match for her.
She would have a husband who would cherish her dearly.
At this moment in time, she feared him.
She kept him at a careful, respectful distance.
Sure enough — his fingers had not yet reached her face when he caught the look that flitted through Xi Rongyan's eyes: a trembling, panicked gaze turned toward him.
Just as in his former life, when she would always look at him with that expression of frightened alarm.
She even stepped back a small pace.
Wei Qi pressed down the shadow that stirred briefly in his heart, and smiled, withdrawing his hand. "Is Rongyan going to the Empress Dowager's palace?"
Xi Rongyan was momentarily unsettled by the Emperor's form of address.
Though the Empress Dowager was her father's elder sister, the Emperor was not the Empress Dowager's own son. She and the current Emperor had exchanged only a handful of words. Though she had often visited the palace to accompany the Empress Dowager, the only prince she had become acquainted with was the former Crown Prince — she was not familiar with the other princes.
She and the Emperor were hardly acquainted at all. For him to address her this way left her faintly uneasy.
She lowered her head and replied with heightened deference, not daring to look up.
Wei Qi nodded and simply said, "Then go ahead, Rongyan."
Beneath the imposing presence of Wei Qi's tall frame, Xi Rongyan felt an inexplicable relief. She quickly took her leave and turned to go.
Yet the gaze on her back was like needles. She kept her hands composed, even as her palms grew damp with sweat.
Wei Qi clasped his hands behind his back and watched Xi Rongyan's proper, cautious retreating figure.
She had always been the very model of a noble young lady — her bearing and deportment never out of place.
Reserved and modest, yet warm and approachable.
With just that hint of timidity and rule-abidance.
In his former life, even after her husband had died, she had chosen to cling to that cold spirit tablet rather than accept his offer of remarriage.
He pressed his lips together. The last trace of warmth on his cold, severe expression dissipated.
Beside him, Eunuch Gao bent low and murmured in Wei Qi's ear, "Your Majesty, what shall be done with these two?"
Wei Qi's ice-cold gaze swept over the two court ladies kneeling on the ground, their mouths stuffed shut. With calm indifference, he let fall a single cruel sentence: "Fifty blows."
He turned, and mounted the palanquin once more.
The two court ladies kneeling on the ground began to shake all over at once, kowtowing in desperate, silent pleas for mercy — fifty blows would mean their lives.
Eunuch Gao, afraid their muffled cries would reach Xi Rongyan ahead, had the men drag them away at once.
He glanced at the bloodstained marks on the ground they had left behind and could not help but sigh.
They had only themselves to blame for wagging their tongues — and in front of the Fourth Young Miss of the Xi family, no less. They had thrown away their lives for nothing.
The Emperor had never been a merciful man.

chapters.title: Would You Like to Enter the Palace?
chapters.content:
As Xi Rongyan stepped into Cining Palace, the Empress Dowager smiled and beckoned to her at once. "Rongyan, come sit beside me."
Only then did a smile touch Xi Rongyan's face, and she settled herself obediently at the Empress Dowager's side.
The Empress Dowager took Xi Rongyan's hands and studied her face carefully, then sighed. "You look thinner. Is it the grief over the Gu family matter?"
"Or the talk going around outside?"
Xi Rongyan lowered her gaze and replied honestly, in a small voice: "The rumors outside have been painful to hear, and I truly am grieving over what happened to the Gu family."
She paused, then added softly, "Yunyu gege was such a gentle young man. He did not deserve to meet this end."
"Perhaps I really did bring misfortune upon him."
The Empress Dowager frowned. "How can you believe such nonsense?"
"When you were a small child, a great master told your fortune — it was an excellent fate. How could you possibly be a blight upon your husband?"
She patted Xi Rongyan's hand. "You need not worry about a match. I will select a good one for you."
Then the Empress Dowager looked at Xi Rongyan with a warm smile. "Or is there someone you yourself favor?"
Xi Rongyan still felt that it was too heartless to begin arranging a new betrothal so soon after her intended husband had just passed. She felt wretched even thinking of it.
She looked up at the Empress Dowager. "Aunt, please let the matter of an engagement wait a little longer. I am not in any hurry."
The Empress Dowager's elegantly groomed fingers brushed over Xi Rongyan's soft skin and she sighed. "Rongyan, a matter of marriage cannot wait."
Xi Rongyan said nothing, and gripped her embroidered handkerchief tightly. The hundred flowers and butterflies on it vanished beneath her tapered fingertips, pressing out of shape.
Then the Empress Dowager's quiet voice reached her ears: "Ren Ziqi, the eldest legitimate grandson of the Xuanyi Marquisate, is exactly the right age for you — three years your senior. He passed the imperial examinations last year as an Tanhua scholar and now serves in the Hanlin Academy."
"He is said to be upright in conduct, warm and courteous in manner, and the Xuanyi Marquisate is known for its good family values. The older generation may not hold the highest positions, but their descendants have all distinguished themselves — and Ren Ziqi is the most outstanding of them all."
"You would certainly live a contented life married to him."
The Empress Dowager smiled again. "His looks are also first-rate — how many young ladies sighed over him when he rode through the streets as an examination graduate?"
"You are sure to like him as well."
Xi Rongyan felt that many things in life were beyond her control, and her marriage had never once been hers to decide.
Both engagements had been arranged by her father with the family's interests in mind, and neither time had he ever asked what she herself wished.
She could not refute her aunt. She only said quietly, "Aunt, could you let me think about it a little longer?"
"I still do not wish to be betrothed this quickly. At least let three months pass, until the matter of the Gu family is no longer on people's lips."
The Empress Dowager understood what Xi Rongyan meant. She patted her hand and looked at her with tender pity. "I have watched you grow up. From childhood, you were gentle and obedient. I know your heart is good — the people outside do not understand you, but I know you best of all."
"If a small sparrow died, you would grieve for it — how much more so for a person?"
"That young Gu man was, in truth, good to you. You two were well-matched. It is only that your bond was shallow — there is no other cause."
"Do not dwell on it."
As she spoke, she gazed at Xi Rongyan's face — the dark hair coiled elegantly, two long jade hairpins set plainly across it, the jade glimmering softly, her figure all jade-boned and ice-clear, red lips and gleaming teeth. She was, by nature, a rare and striking beauty.
Whoever she married in the end, with that face and figure and warm, sensible disposition, she was sure to be cherished and well tended by her husband.
She would pass her life smoothly and without strife.
It was a pity that both betrothals had ended badly.
She felt a swell of compassion, and lowered her voice: "Actually, after the Gu family incident, your father discussed with me the possibility of letting you enter the palace. With this affair having happened and so much talk circulating, arranging a new match truly is difficult."
"But I did not agree to it at the time."
The Empress Dowager tightened her grip on Xi Rongyan's hands and asked, "Now I am asking you directly: would you like to enter the palace?"
"If you are willing, I can protect you here."
Xi Rongyan was startled. The image of her encounter with the Emperor just moments ago suddenly flashed through her mind.
She had not dared to look up at the Emperor's face, but she had felt the weighty authority that pressed from him. Though his tone just now had been gentle, seeming unlike the cold, erratic ruler of rumor, something about him still filled her with an inexplicable dread.
She shook her head. "If I enter the palace, I will not be able to return home often to see my family. I do not wish to enter."
The Empress Dowager nodded and patted Xi Rongyan's hand with a sigh. "Very well."
"I know your nature. The scheming and maneuvering of the women in the inner palace — you would not fare well in it. You are my most beloved niece, and I will find you a harmonious and fitting match."
"Afterward, I will summon someone from the Xuanyi Marquisate and speak to them properly."
Xi Rongyan felt a warmth rise to her eyes. She nodded in willing obedience. "I will follow whatever arrangements Aunt decides upon."
Only then did the Empress Dowager nod, reassured. She asked after Xi Rongyan's mother's illness.
The two of them sat together talking, and before they knew it, it was midday.
Xi Rongyan stayed through the noon meal with the Empress Dowager, then sat a while longer in conversation before taking her leave.
She stepped out of Cining Palace and back onto the palace corridors. The sky had grown heavy.
The third month carried a lingering chill. Cold wind crept in at her collar, and Xi Rongyan felt a faint shiver. The fingers she held outstretched had gone stiff with cold.
Her mind began to wander idly — she thought of the hand warmer she would hold when she got home, of sitting before the brazier with a book, of drinking a cup of hot tea.
Yet, inexplicably, midway along the path a court lady came rushing out of a side hall carrying a bucket of water — and promptly splashed it all over Xi Rongyan's clothing.
The pale mountain-color fabric clung to her skin in dark, spreading patches.
The head attendant escorting Xi Rongyan immediately stepped forward, her expression severe. "Which palace are you from? Who is your head attendant?"
The court lady knelt on the ground, her face drained of color, trembling so badly she seemed unable to form words.
Seeing the girl in such a state of terror, Xi Rongyan thought: though she was cold, she would soon be out of the palace and in the carriage, where she would warm up — there was no need to make things difficult for this girl who appeared to be so very young.
That was a very large bucket of water, and she was such a slight, thin thing. She must have had her own difficulties.
Xi Rongyan said softly to the attendant beside her, "I am perfectly fine — it is only the hem of my skirt that is wet. It is nothing serious. Shall we go?"
No sooner had the words left her lips than a dark-blue figure came hurrying toward her and came to stand before her. "May I ask, are you the Fourth Young Miss of the Xi family?"
He then gave the kneeling court lady a kick and bowed politely to Xi Rongyan. "This court lady is a palace maid from Baohua Hall. His Majesty instructed her to sweep and air out the rooms here for use as a book storage. I came to check on whether the cleaning was done — and instead witnessed this maid's intrusion upon the Fourth Young Miss."
"She has offended a person of standing. I leave her entirely to the Fourth Young Miss's disposal."
Xi Rongyan recognized that the eunuch before her was Gao Yi, the Emperor's personal attendant. Since she had no wish to make things difficult for anyone, she replied in a gentle, soft voice: "In truth it cannot be blamed on her. I did not see her coming when I passed. I would ask Chief Gao to show leniency."
Gao Yi could not help but smile at Xi Rongyan. "The Fourth Young Miss is truly kind and benevolent. His Majesty is also a benevolent and generous lord — he never punishes servants harshly. This is quite in keeping with His Majesty's wishes."
He turned to the court lady at his feet. "Get up and go change your clothes, then return to your duties."
Xi Rongyan let out a quiet breath of relief. Yet she had heard the Emperor described as unpredictable, cold, and severe — it was not at all what she would have expected of someone so lenient with those beneath him.
This matter being settled, she made to bid Chief Gao farewell — but the Chief stopped her again. "Fourth Young Miss, please follow me to the hall just ahead and change your clothing. It is not far."
Xi Rongyan quickly declined. "I thank Chief Gao for the kind thought, but my clothing is only a little damp. It is truly no great matter."
She prepared to excuse herself.
Chief Gao anxiously stepped into her path, his face full of consternation. "His Majesty is a person of ceremonious propriety and magnanimity. The Fourth Young Miss is the Empress Dowager's own beloved niece. If he learns that such a thing befell the Fourth Young Miss in the palace, only to let her leave in this state, he will be distressed — and ashamed to face the Empress Dowager."
"We servants below will be unable to eat or sleep in peace."
Xi Rongyan had only thought it a small matter, yet here was Chief Gao making it sound gravely serious. She quickly said, "I will not mention this incident to the Empress Dowager. You may set your mind at ease, Chief Gao."
Chief Gao's expression fell. "Even if the Fourth Young Miss says nothing, we servants are overcome with guilt, and His Majesty will come to know of it."
And with that, he made to prostrate himself deeply before Xi Rongyan. "I beg the Fourth Young Miss not to put us in an impossible position."
Chief Gao was the Emperor's own close personal eunuch — Xi Rongyan could not possibly allow him to bow to her. She quickly caught his arm. "Since it is Chief Gao's kind intention, I will accept."
She then turned to the head attendant beside her and said, "Attendant, please go back and report to the Empress Dowager. I will leave once I have changed my clothing."
The head attendant glanced at Gao Yi, then said politely, "Chief Gao, once the Fourth Young Miss has changed and is safely on her way, please send someone to let us know."
Chief Gao smiled readily. "Rest assured — we would not dare be negligent with the Fourth Young Miss."
Only then did the attendant take her leave with ease.
Xi Rongyan followed Chief Gao ahead, and it was indeed only a few steps before they arrived.
But as Xi Rongyan looked up at the hall sign and read "Baohua Hall," she suddenly recalled that Chief Gao had just said the court lady was from Baohua Hall, and that he himself had come from Baohua Hall — did that mean the Emperor was also in Baohua Hall?

chapters.title: Bumping Into the Emperor
chapters.content:
Xi Rongyan's heart leapt into her throat. She was about to ask Chief Gao, but when she turned, the Chief had already vanished from sight. Behind her, the court lady urged her on: "Fourth Young Miss, please go inside. Chief Gao has gone to have clothing fetched for you."
Xi Rongyan, seeing the court lady press her with such urgency and feeling the cold of her water-soaked garments acutely in the lingering spring chill, stepped inside.
Once in the hall, a court lady led Xi Rongyan into a room and asked her to wait a moment.
The room held a burning charcoal brazier, and it was considerably warmer inside.
But why was only this room lit with a brazier, and with no one inside?
Though puzzled, she was cold, and drew close to the brazier to sit and warm her hands. She looked around the room.
Along two walls ran floor-to-ceiling bookshelves packed with volumes, and the air carried the subtle fragrance of dragon's musk incense mingled with the scent of old books — a combination that made one inexplicably drowsy.
Outside, rain seemed to have started up again, a soft, hushing sound. She thought idly that on her way back she would likely get the hem of her skirt wet all over again.
Then Xi Rongyan startled — how was it that there was not a single palace servant in the room? Not even Baozhu, who had been walking behind her, was anywhere to be seen. She called out softly, "Baozhu."
The thin sound of her voice echoed through the empty chamber, meeting no reply.
A small flutter of anxiety rose in her chest. She got to her feet, wanting to go and look.
She rose from the chair and walked briskly toward the entrance. Perhaps because she was moving a little too quickly, she had scarcely passed the screen when she walked straight into someone.
Her body stumbled back a step instinctively, but a warm, firm hand caught her swiftly at the waist.
The scent of dragon's musk enveloped Xi Rongyan. She stared, momentarily dazed, at the golden dragon embroidered on the dark garment before her — and in a beat of slow confusion, looked up to meet a pair of deep eyes, filled with steady concern.
The warmth at her waist lifted quickly, and the figure stepped back a respectful distance. A low, measured voice followed: "I heard a palace maid below had caused an inconvenience for Rongyan. As I happened to be here reading, I came to see how you were."
Wei Qi then asked quietly, "Is Rongyan all right?"
Xi Rongyan came to herself at the sound of Wei Qi's low voice, and quickly turned pale as she sank into a curtsy. "This subject is fine. It is only this subject who just now intruded upon Your Majesty — I beg Your Majesty's pardon."
But a sound of gentle commiseration came from above, and before Xi Rongyan could react, a warmth settled over her. Looking down, she saw a pair of elegant, slender fingers — and realized the Emperor had draped a bright-yellow cloak embroidered with golden dragons across her shoulders.
The Emperor's low voice came from just beside her ear, his breath warm against her face: "No need for formalities. Take care not to let the cold into your body."
His gentle tone set her heart racing in spite of herself. Xi Rongyan suppressed the urge to step back, and looked up at the Emperor. "Your Majesty is kind, but this subject is of humble station and would not dare to use Your Majesty's belongings."
She reached up to remove the cloak from her shoulders as she spoke.
But a broad hand came down over her fingers at once, and she looked up to meet the Emperor's low, steady gaze. "It is only a cloak. Would you have me stand by and watch while you are still wet?"
Xi Rongyan stood still, then saw Wei Qi withdraw his hand just as quickly. His gaze dropped to her once more. "Your maidservant has gone to the Imperial Wardrobe to fetch shoes to fit your size. Clothing will be brought shortly — you need not worry."
"Nor will anyone come in."
With that, Wei Qi stepped back and, his gaze not once straying to any other part of Xi Rongyan, turned and walked out.
Xi Rongyan still stood where she was, blankly. Then the charcoal in the brazier crackled suddenly behind her, and she gathered herself. She thought of the Emperor's calm and gentle manner just now — it truly was nothing like the cold tyrant in the rumors.
Her heart settled. She turned back to wait.
A court lady soon brought in a fresh set of clothing and shoes.
Not seeing her own maidservant, Xi Rongyan asked softly, "Is my maidservant outside?"
The court lady stood before her with great deference. "Baozhu fell on the way. Chief Gao sent someone to take Baozhu to the Imperial Physicians' Office first."
Xi Rongyan startled again. "How did she fall?"
The court lady shook her head. "Perhaps the rain made the path slippery. Baozhu was in a bit of a hurry."
Xi Rongyan had no choice but to nod. She went into the inner room to change, without needing any help from the court ladies.
When she came out again, the outer hall was empty and still.
Baozhu had not yet returned. The only one waiting outside was a court lady with her head lowered.
Xi Rongyan stood at the window, watching the sky slowly deepen. The rain was falling again, fine and thin. A restlessness grew in her heart.
She had been delayed, and it was getting late.
She turned and asked the court lady standing nearby to go to the Imperial Physicians' Office and inquire after her maidservant.
The court lady agreed at once and hurried out.
The sound of rain beat upon the steps outside. Cold air seeped in. She knew it was not proper to remain in this hall indefinitely.
Perhaps it would be better to go to the Physicians' Office herself and find her maidservant, and then they could leave together.
With that thought, she turned to the court lady left nearby and asked, "Is the Emperor here?"
The court lady replied with great respect: "His Majesty is inside reading."
She looked up at Xi Rongyan. "Shall I show you the way?"
Xi Rongyan reflected that the Emperor was present, and so she must certainly take her leave of him properly.
She nodded, and followed the court lady deeper into the hall.
Baohua Hall was vast, bookshelves stretching in every direction. When at last they reached the far end, the court lady stopped outside and said softly to Xi Rongyan, "His Majesty is inside."
Xi Rongyan listened to the silence within, hesitating about whether to go in.
Would she be disturbing him at this hour?
She was still deliberating when Chief Gao stepped silently out from inside. He smiled and murmured, "Is the Fourth Young Miss here to see His Majesty?"
Seeing Chief Gao appear, Xi Rongyan could only nod. She lowered her voice and asked, "Is this a convenient moment?"
"If it is, I would be grateful if Chief Gao would announce my arrival."
Chief Gao smiled. "Of course. The Fourth Young Miss may go right in."
And with that, he stepped aside.

chapters.title: It Seems You Fear Me
chapters.content:
It was Xi Rongyan's first time in this particular place, yet a strange sensation rose in her — both familiar and frightening — and for one fleeting moment she had the urge to turn around and leave.
She did not know why. Perhaps it was the dim light throughout the hall, with the only brightness pooled at the far end where the Emperor sat.
Yet even that brightness flickered — half the Emperor's face lay hidden in shadow, his tall figure a dark mass within the dimness, like a predator waiting in the dark, silently watching for his quarry.
Something flashed through her mind without warning. She stared blankly at the silhouette behind the rosewood writing desk, and for a moment seemed to see herself kneeling on the floor in disarray, her body afire, begging the man high above her to save her.
Her heart hammered, and the dread she felt only sharpened.
Beside her, Chief Gao murmured softly, "Is something wrong, Miss Xi?"
Xi Rongyan came back to herself and walked forward with her head lowered.
When she was five paces from the writing desk, she stopped, performed a proper and measured greeting, and paid her respects to the Emperor.
Wei Qi, who had been obscured in shadow, slowly allowed his face to emerge into the lamplight.
He set down the scroll in his hands, the gold of his crown gleaming faintly.
Those sharp, all-perceiving eyes now rested on Xi Rongyan as he said in a low voice, "Rongyan. Sit."
His slender finger pointed to the cushion across from him. The voice was gentle, and yet Xi Rongyan felt an undeniable, irresistible pressure behind it.
She did not dare look up. With perfect propriety, she crossed and sat down on the cushion before her.
She placed her hands tidily on her knees, though her palms had broken out in cold sweat.
Wei Qi lifted his hand to pour tea for Xi Rongyan, as though he could read what was in her mind. He said calmly, "Your maidservant has sprained her ankle. Physician Wang at the Imperial Physicians' Office is resetting the bone for her now."
"I have already sent someone to look after her. Once she has been wrapped up, they will help her to come and find you."
With that, Wei Qi's gaze settled on Xi Rongyan's lowered eyes and brows.
He gave a small smile and placed the white jade teacup in front of her. "Rongyan, it seems you fear me."
The fingers before her were pale and slender, and in the dim, indistinct light, unaccountably unsettling.
She quickly reached out with both hands to take the cup, answering with composed propriety: "This subject holds Your Majesty in reverence and would not dare act beyond her station."
But Wei Qi's fingers occupied the full span of the cup. Despite her care, her fingers still brushed against his.
She could not help but tremble. The tea in the jade cup shivered and spilled, wetting Wei Qi's fingers.
Xi Rongyan's color drained. She was about to look up to offer an apology, but instead met a pair of fathomless, deep-set eyes.
Wei Qi's features were not those of a gentle man — his brows slanted in sharp angles, his lips thin, his eyes long, his countenance striking and proud yet carrying an air of cool indifference. Even with laughter in his eyes, one could not help but feel trepidation.
Her grandmother had always said: the face reflects the heart.
A cold and flinty man will have cold and flinty features.
A man of warm compassion will look gentle, like jade in water.
And Wei Qi was clearly not the gentle-looking kind.
In truth, Xi Rongyan had had little contact with Wei Qi before. They had only crossed paths a handful of times.
Wei Qi had been enfeoffed as a prince at fifteen and dispatched to the northern territories to hold the frontier, returning only when the previous Emperor had suffered a severe stroke and was gravely ill.
Word had it that during nearly ten years in the north, his hands had been stained with a great deal of blood, and his name had become known for ruthlessness.
It was also said that the previous Emperor had once summoned Wei Qi alone, and that on that very day, the previous Emperor had died. When Wei Qi and the eunuch at the Emperor's side came out, the head eunuch had transmitted the former Emperor's verbal decree naming Wei Qi Crown Prince.
Her father had once described the scene: Wei Qi had brought soldiers from the north to station themselves outside the palace gates — ostensibly to guard against unrest, though the move had ensured that no minister of the court dared to object.
Some said Wei Qi harbored wolfish ambitions and had murdered his father to seize the throne.
Though none would dare speak it openly, this kind of talk still circulated in private.
Perhaps it was these rumors that had left a mark on Xi Rongyan's heart and made her wary of Wei Qi.
Now, she knelt before the Emperor, holding the cup with both hands, and quickly asked forgiveness. "This subject has behaved improperly — I beg Your Majesty's pardon."
Wei Qi looked quietly at Xi Rongyan kneeling before him.
Her slender neck, white as porcelain in the lamplight. Her delicate eyes and brows, lowered like a bow of the moon.
The sapphire-blue silk of her skirt caught the light at every fold. Her wrists, held up dutifully with the cup, were half-bared at the sleeve — a jade bracelet glinting at each wrist.
Wei Qi lounged against the small side table in an unhurried posture, his long fingers tapping on his drawn-up knee, his scrutinizing gaze never once leaving Xi Rongyan.
Her decorum.
It was, in truth, fear.
Wei Qi was silent. He straightened himself with perfect composure, bent down, and grasped Xi Rongyan's hand — a note of faint regret in his quiet voice: "Why must Rongyan fear me so?"
"Think of me as your elder cousin. There is no need for this formality and distance."
His breath was close, and the air all around was the fragrance of dragon's musk. She kept her head low, her posture still deferential. "Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven. This subject would not dare overstep."
Had Xi Rongyan looked up in that moment, she would have seen the cold that moved across Wei Qi's face.
His thumb traced slowly across Xi Rongyan's fingers — and then, quickly, he released her. He smiled, still easy-tempered and low: "Since Rongyan is so distant with me, I will not insist."
"You may rise."
Hearing this, Xi Rongyan felt a nervous tremor in her heart. She gave her thanks and stood.
She struggled inwardly — how, exactly, was she supposed to behave toward the Emperor?
Did the Emperor truly wish for someone to be close to him as a kinsman would?
Her father and eldest brother had told her the Emperor was the Son of Heaven, a ruler and sovereign — and that only by always treating him as such would one never err.
From childhood, she had kept faithfully to her father's instruction. Not once in all her visits to the palace had she made a mistake.
Even in the Empress Dowager's presence, she had never traded on the favor shown her — never once let her composure slip, never once lost sight of proper rank and decorum.
The hall, filled wall to wall with bookshelves, was dim throughout. Everywhere except the small island of brighter light where they sat lay in blurred shadow.
It was as though there were only the two of them in this place.
The soft patter of rain came from the window outside. Her palms were damp. She could not suppress the rising need to leave this place, so shadowed and unsettling.
But the Emperor across from her spoke first. His voice flowed through the stillness, low and unhurried: "The Empress Dowager has spoken to you about a match?"
Xi Rongyan kept her bearing composed and answered with proper promptness: "She has."
Wei Qi gave an idle, unconcerned smile. "Oh?"
He spoke as though idly leafing through his scroll while making easy, offhanded conversation. He asked, almost as an afterthought: "And which family has the Empress Dowager taken a liking to?"
Xi Rongyan thought for a moment and replied: "The Empress Dowager has not decided yet."
Wei Qi made a sound of acknowledgment, his gaze settling on Xi Rongyan. "And which family do you favor?"
Xi Rongyan lowered her gaze. "The arrangement of this subject's marriage is entirely in my father's hands."
A cold smile curved at the corner of Wei Qi's mouth, and he asked again in a light, casual tone: "Did the breaking of the Gu engagement wound you?"

chapters.title: The Emperor Is Nothing Like the Rumors
chapters.content:
Xi Rongyan had not expected the Emperor to ask her this. Had he heard of it as well?
She weighed the question inwardly, then answered honestly with a nod: "It did."
For she truly was wounded.
The words had scarcely left her lips when she heard a sharp tearing sound — Wei Qi's fingers had split the page of the scroll. She stared, astonished.
Wei Qi caught Xi Rongyan's startled gaze, pressed his lips together, and held back the cold.
He gave a short laugh. "Did I startle you?"
Xi Rongyan shook her head quickly.
Wei Qi nodded, his long fingers drumming against the tabletop. He did not speak again.
A long silence followed.
Outside, the sky had grown very dark. If she did not leave soon, her family would begin to worry.
Wei Qi took in Xi Rongyan's unease, and the shadow in his eyes deepened still.
Just then a eunuch crept in softly and knelt before Wei Qi. "Your Majesty, Baozhu has returned."
Wei Qi's gaze swept across Xi Rongyan's face. Seeing the small sigh of relief she could not hide, his eyes turned cold in the shadows.
He waved his hand, but still rose, watching her. His voice remained gentle: "Rongyan, let us go."
Seeing the Emperor stand, Xi Rongyan quickly followed. "This subject can find my own way back."
Wei Qi stood in front of her, his tall frame casting its shadow over her. He looked down at her clear, pale face and gave a slight smile. "Never mind. I was leaving as well."
He walked ahead, and Xi Rongyan followed a careful pace behind.
In the outer hall, Baozhu saw her mistress come out and hurried over with a glad cry: "Miss!"
Xi Rongyan asked her, "Is your foot all right?"
Baozhu nodded. "It was only a twist. The physician at the Physicians' Office set it and it is fine now."
Xi Rongyan let out a relieved breath.
Wei Qi clasped his hands behind his back, watching this. Then he turned and said quietly to the attendant beside him, "Prepare a palanquin."
Xi Rongyan heard the Emperor's order and quickly turned aside to decline.
Wei Qi looked down at her, his tone a gentle admonition: "It is raining outside, and the palace paths are slippery. Go slowly."
Wei Qi was standing right before her. His shadow fell across her — unexpectedly close, and faintly charged.
Xi Rongyan did not dare refuse again. She agreed at once.
When Eunuch Gao escorted her to the front of the hall, a palanquin was already waiting.
It was Xi Rongyan's first time riding a palanquin within the palace, and she felt somewhat out of her element. But Chief Gao told her it was a gift of the Emperor's favor — rarely bestowed on anyone.
She settled in. Four or five palace servants walked at the side with lanterns raised, and the palanquin moved slowly off into the depths of the corridor.
Gao Yi watched until Xi Rongyan was safely on her way, then let out a full breath of relief and turned back to Baohua Hall.
Wei Qi was standing at the window, clasped hands behind his back, watching the distant light.
In the fine curtain of rain, the figure lit by lantern glow was hazed and indistinct, swaying nearer and farther.
Wei Qi turned his thumb ring over and over. His expression gradually fell still and cold.
Gao Yi stood behind Wei Qi and quietly relayed what Xi Rongyan and the Empress Dowager had discussed in Cining Palace.
Wei Qi's face showed nothing. When Gao Yi reported that Xi Rongyan had refused to enter the palace, the line of his mouth pressed downward.
Gao Yi added with careful deference: "The Empress Dowager also mentioned she favors the second young master of the Xuanyi Marquisate. The Fourth Young Miss seemed agreeable to it."
In that instant, a chill gathered in the air. Gao Yi's heart lurched with fright.
No emotion showed in Wei Qi's cold, thin eyes. He turned and strode out of Baohua Hall.
—
On the other side, as Xi Rongyan came out through the palace gate, she saw a slender figure standing beside her carriage at the gate.
When the figure caught sight of her, he quickly opened an umbrella and came toward her.
Xi Wenli walked to his sister's side and held the paper umbrella over her head, his tone one of concern. "What kept you so long?"
Xi Rongyan walked with her eldest brother toward the carriage, speaking quietly: "I was with Aunt talking a little long today. On my way back this afternoon I had cold water spilled on me by a palace maid."
She gave her brother a rough account of what had happened after.
In the carriage, her brother had prepared a hand warmer for her. She held it to her chest, and warmth crept back into her fingers.
She closed her eyes and thought again of the Emperor's gentle manner today — a little different from what she had imagined.
She could not help but ask her brother, "Does the Emperor have a good temperament?"
Xi Wenli looked at his sister and gave a helpless smile. "Why would you ask that?"
Xi Rongyan lowered her head. The carriage swayed. The jade pin in her hair had come slightly loose.
She said softly, "I saw the Emperor today. He seemed very gentle — not so severe at all."
"Not like the Emperor in the rumors."
Xi Wenli served as a Secretariat Gentleman in the Secretariat, overseeing the Four Repository Collections. Though his position was near the center of power, he had little involvement in court affairs and few occasions to see the Emperor. Yet surrounded by the scions of great families, with his extensive connections, he knew something of the new Emperor's nature in the three years since his accession.
He spoke to Xi Rongyan seriously, in a low voice: "The Emperor keeps himself very much to himself — his temperament is rarely revealed to the outside world. But he is far from a gentle man."
"In three years on the throne, he has elevated a new class of scholars to balance the old great families. And in his years as a border prince in the north, he crushed the northern tribes in blood — his hands are stained with countless lives. How could he be a gentle man?"
"When the previous Emperor lay ill, three princes watched and waited. Yet it was the Emperor who ascended in the end."
"A gentle man could never occupy the seat he holds today."
"His Majesty's mind is like the ocean. Do not take liberties with him."
Xi Rongyan listened, then quietly nodded. The earrings brushed against her face, and she said no more.
When the carriage came to a stop, her brother draped a cloak over her shoulders and said softly, "Go rest. I will give Mother a report."
Xi Rongyan murmured her assent, wrapped the cloak around herself, and turned to walk back to her own courtyard.
Back in her rooms, she bathed and sat on the daybed cradling her cat, lost in thought. On a whim, she asked Baozhu how she had come to fall earlier.
Baozhu was pressing a warm cloth and a hand warmer against Xi Rongyan's hair to help it dry. At the question, she replied, "I really couldn't say, Miss. I was walking along and then something seemed to knock me at the heel, and I went down."
"There was a court lady nearby who caught me just in time. It hurt so badly that I forgot to look and see what had hit me."
Xi Rongyan nodded and asked, "Is it better now?"
Baozhu smiled. "Much better. The medicine from the palace really is something — one application and the pain was gone."
Xi Rongyan's hand worked absently at the cat's ear.
When her hair was dry, she lay forward on the daybed against the soft pillows and watched Baozhu tidy the books at the side of the bed. After a moment she said softly, "I don't want to marry anymore."
Baozhu nearly startled at these words. Her hands stilled. She looked up to see Xi Rongyan's dark hair framing her small face, her beautiful eyes dim. Her lips parted again, murmuring, "Is it all right for me to say that?"
Her voice was very quiet. "I've truly been thinking — could it be that Young Master Gu's death was because of me, that I am a curse upon my intended?"
Baozhu was afraid her mistress would sink again into sorrow, and quickly said, "Miss, please do not think that way. It is not your fault."
Xi Rongyan covered her face with the brocade quilt, her fingers pressed around the peach blossom hairpin that Gu Yunyu had once given her as a token of his affection, kept beneath her pillow. A muffled voice came from within: "Perhaps."
After a long silence, another small voice drifted out: "I always feel so wretched."
"But they all say to move past it. Yunyu gege vanished so suddenly — can it really be put aside so easily?"
Baozhu did not know how to offer comfort. She could only keep quietly vigil, and it was not until there was no more sound from beneath the quilt that she lifted it gently.
The one inside was already asleep, eyes rimmed red.
Baozhu sighed in silence, let the curtain fall back, and slipped softly out of the room.

chapters.title: A Marriage Proposal
chapters.content:
Several more days passed. The long, overcast rain came to an end, and a few threads of pale sunlight broke through.
Xi Rongyan was sitting at the edge of the back courtyard pavilion, gazing at the fish in the water in a daze, when she saw her mother's nanny come to call her to the main courtyard.
In the main hall, Lady Xie smiled and beckoned Xi Rongyan over to choose fabric: "Spring has opened and the weather is warming. Pick out the colors you like — I'll have you two spring outfits made."
Then she looked at her daughter with a warm smile: "The Flower Festival is in a few days. You can wear one of them when I take you to meet the Marchioness of the Xuanyi Marquisate."
Xi Rongyan startled. "There really is no need to hurry."
Lady Xie smiled. "Do you think there are no matchmakers calling on the Xuanyi Marquisate?"
"I have made inquiries. Many families have their eye on a connection there — the young man is both distinguished and upright, and absolutely the finest candidate."
"Yesterday the Empress Dowager saw your father — she indicated it should be settled soon. What if the Xuanyi Marquisate takes another girl first? Would you not regret that?"
"Ren Ziqi is exactly twenty this year — the perfect age to be betrothed."
"If they are agreeable, the Empress Dowager will issue the decree for you."
Xi Rongyan had been about to say that passing on this opportunity would be no great loss. But seeing the lingering pallor of illness still on her mother's face, and the worried look in her eyes, she swallowed the words and gave a quiet nod.
She reached out and selected a length of lotus-white rain-silk embroidered with orchids.
Lady Xie smiled. "Pale, clean colors suit you best. Very good."
She told the servants to have it made up.
On the day of the Flower Festival, Xi Rongyan and her mother boarded the carriage together.
On the Flower Festival, the imperial pleasure garden, Xiuyuan, was opened to the public. The ladies of noble and official families all gathered there, and the Empress presided over the occasion.
There was much to delight in — drinking the Hundred Flower Wine, wearing the Hundred Flower Crown, chasing butterflies, eating at the flower banquet.
Xi Rongyan had come in previous years. Last year she had missed it entirely, having fallen ill with a cold just those few days.
The garden was enormous. Inside were only women — peach blossoms blazed, and petals carpeted the ground. Young ladies in their finest came in clusters of three and five to chase butterflies, and laughter rang on all sides.
The moment Xi Rongyan arrived, scrutinizing glances settled on her from every direction, accompanied by lowered voices.
Some were gleeful. Some mocking. Some pitying.
Xi Rongyan pressed her fingers tight around the painted fan of mountain camellia and stayed close behind her mother.
Lady Xie had been acquainted with the Xuanyi Marquisate in earlier years, and so she brought Xi Rongyan toward the pavilion where the Marchioness sat.
The Empress Dowager had not yet issued her decree, and the Xuanyi Marquisate had not yet been summoned. Lady Xie wished to feel out the Marquisate's intentions first.
Wei Qi stood at a distance in an upstairs gallery, watching as Madam Xi led Xi Rongyan to sit and chat with the Xuanyi Marquisate in the pavilion below. His eyes narrowed to a dangerous slant.
A cold, faint smile curved at the corner of his mouth. Then he turned away.
Xi Rongyan glanced to one side, searching for the Gu family. Seeing no one from there, a pang twisted in her heart.
Then her mother was drawing her forward to exchange greetings with the Marchioness of Xuanyi, Lady Lin, and she gathered herself.
Lady Lin looked Xi Rongyan over. The girl stood there, graceful and quiet — one glance told you she was learned, well-mannered, a daughter of good family in every sense.
She knew of Xi Rongyan, said by rumor to be the very model of a noble young lady. Seeing her now, she found the reputation well-deserved.
And her voice, when she spoke, was like pearls dropping into water. The plain jade pin in her hair, the lotus-white half-collared robe, set off by the lustrous pearl drops swaying at her ears — truly very fine to look upon.
Delicate and white, like smoke draped over a blooming face.
Lady Lin smiled and nodded. "People outside say the Fourth Young Miss of the Xi family is a girl of rare gifts and grace — and so she is."
Lady Xie sighed regretfully. "It is only a pity that her marriages have not gone smoothly."
"And now others have been spreading gossip."
Lady Lin looked at Lady Xie. "None of that matters. I do not believe any of it."
"This business about cursing one's husband — no sensible person believes such things."
Lady Xie brightened, and seemed to sorrow all at once. "Sister is so clear-eyed."
Lady Lin smiled. "Oh, I wouldn't say that. I have never once visited a temple to pray for fate."
"Fate rests in a person's own hands, I say. I have saved many lives in my time."
"Even those already at the gates of death. Fate is not as fixed as they say."
Lady Xie was surprised.
She suddenly remembered — Lady Lin was not from a prominent family. In earlier days she had been a lady physician who, by a twist of fate, had saved the Marquis's life and won his eye. The wedding had been a grand affair, and she had married into the Marquisate in some style.
Perhaps her disbelief in fate was genuine.
That was good news.
Then a stir broke out nearby. A line of palace ladies came carrying bamboo sticks, distributing them to the women present — it was time for the verse-composing game.
The Empress would choose the three finest verses, and award each one a gift. The winner of the top prize would have the Empress herself place the Hundred Flower Crown upon her head.
This game had been held in previous years too. The woman who received the Hundred Flower Crown from the Empress's own hands could then make a request of the Empress.
The consorts of the inner palace could also participate. It was all quite festive.
A serving girl's tray came to Xi Rongyan. She took a stick, but had no heart for verse-composing. She dashed something down carelessly — enough to count as participation.
With the rumors surrounding her, she did not want to draw attention. Whatever she wrote, it was certainly not going to be selected.
After a while, the winning verses were announced, and all those who had participated moved in that direction.
Lady Xie was deep in warm conversation with the Marchioness, and sent Xi Rongyan off with her maidservants to enjoy the spectacle.
Xi Rongyan had thought she certainly would not be chosen, and had little wish to go. But she saw the maidservant at her side craning her neck toward the crowd, clearly wanting to see who had won top prize.
In the end she rose and went to stand at the back of the gathering with her servant.
The Empress stood on the raised dais. A palace lady beside her held a tray bearing the winning verses.
Three names were announced in succession, and young women went forward to receive their prizes amid the envious eyes of the crowd.
The winner of the top prize also received the Hundred Flower Crown placed on her head by the Empress herself and the Empress's blessing.
Under ordinary circumstances this would have been the end, but then it was announced that there was one more prize — flower-brewed wine, specially awarded by the Empress.
This flower wine was made only in the palace. It was extraordinarily precious, its making elaborate — a single jug required hundreds of catties of blossoms.
It was said that one cup could clear the humors, beautify the complexion, and leave a lingering fragrance on the body for days.
And this year it was being offered as a prize for the very first time, stirring a wave of anticipation among the ladies.
The senior court attendant then announced five names in total — and among them, to everyone's astonishment, was Xi Rongyan.
Xi Rongyan startled. She could not have imagined being selected.
Seeing the others all come forward, she had no choice but to steel herself and do the same.
The attendant brought the wine before her and said with a smile, "Congratulations, Fourth Young Miss Xi. Your verse has caught the Empress's eye. This Hundred Flower Wine is the finest thing for one's health — even Her Majesty herself rarely has opportunity to taste it."
Xi Rongyan stared at the wine cup before her, at a loss. She could not drink a single drop of alcohol.
Only those close to her knew this. But she could not refuse the Empress's gift.
Baozhu and Chunyun, standing behind her, were worried, yet dared not intervene.
The other women being rewarded alongside her had already drunk theirs. Xi Rongyan tightened her fingers, and under the eyes of the assembled crowd, lifted the cup with quiet composure and drank it down.
Not a trace of impropriety showed in her bearing.
She then gave her thanks to the Empress.
But the moment she finished, her head began to swim. She gripped Baozhu's hand tight, and her figure wavered.
The palace lady before her, sensing that something was wrong, said with concern: "The Hundred Flower Wine is a touch potent. If the Miss is feeling unwell, Qingshan Pavilion just ahead is set aside for ladies to rest in. All the guests today are ladies — the Miss may go there without worry."
Xi Rongyan knew that if she lost herself to drink in public her dignity would suffer. She thanked the lady and quickly asked Chunyun to go and inform her mother, then let Baozhu lead her toward Qingshan Pavilion.
The wine had already begun to riot through her body. She exhaled, feeling heat spreading over her skin.
Baozhu knew what her mistress was like in drink better than anyone — she did not dare delay even a moment.
Fortunately, Qingshan Pavilion was truly close. Xi Rongyan summoned her last thread of clarity to look up, saw the words "Qingshan Pavilion" above the lintel, and let out a breath of relief — and let Baozhu guide her inside.
But inside Qingshan Pavilion there was not a soul. Baozhu had only just helped Xi Rongyan onto a daybed and set her down when Xi Rongyan, her senses already blurring, clung to Baozhu, her eyes swimming with tears: "Don't go."

chapters.title: I Have Seen You in My Dreams
chapters.content:
Baozhu had served Xi Rongyan for years, and there was nothing she dreaded more than her mistress and wine.
The occasional tipple of rice wine on a winter night was enough to turn her into a completely different person before long.
She would cling to Baozhu and refuse to let go, then refuse to sleep properly and insist on wandering outside — demanding, in the dead of winter, to go and pick flowers.
It never took less than half a shi of coaxing before the ordeal was over, and by the time it was, she would have forgotten all of it.
After that, Xi Rongyan herself had learned to be careful about wine. No matter how much she might want a taste, she limited herself to a sip or two of rice wine at most. Fruit wine she had not touched since.
The court lady had just said the Hundred Flower Wine was potent — and Baozhu truly did not know how long her mistress would be in this state.
Xi Rongyan was again burying her face in Baozhu's arms, murmuring about wanting to play the qin. Baozhu could only manage helplessly — where on earth would she find a qin at this moment?
The figure in her arms had gone boneless, practically all her weight draped over Baozhu, yet she refused to lie still and kept squirming — she would absolutely not cooperate and sleep on the daybed. Baozhu was already half exhausted.
Just then a noise came from behind. Baozhu turned — and nearly shocked herself unconscious.
There stood the Emperor, wearing a deep black crane-robe embroidered with gold dragons, his chest half bared, still dripping. As though he had just stepped from a bath.
His features were sharp and cold, the full imperial authority bearing down in a wave of chill. His indifferent gaze swept their way — and Baozhu's heart quailed.
Then Chief Gao beside the Emperor snapped sternly: "His Majesty rests here — who dares intrude?"
Baozhu's legs gave out, and she went straight to her knees, trembling head to toe.
She stammered through her explanation, cold sweat streaming down her brow.
How could she possibly have imagined the Emperor would be here?
And all the while her young mistress was completely unaware of what had happened — kneeling there, she was already tugging at Baozhu to get up and go fetch the qin.
Baozhu was half ready to prostrate herself before this impossible young lady and beg — she was terrified that in her state Xi Rongyan might do something improper in the Emperor's presence, which would be a catastrophe.
Wei Qi's gaze fell to Xi Rongyan, kneeling on the ground with her head buried in Baozhu's arms.
Her white face peeked through strands of hair, a flush upon her cheeks, the jade earrings swaying in disarray, her garments faintly disheveled.
Murmuring incoherent words.
His silent, proud expression gave nothing away. Yet Wei Qi stepped forward, coming to stand before the two women kneeling on the ground.
He clasped his hands behind his back, his long eyes cast downward. He glanced at Baozhu and spoke in a tone that revealed nothing: "She is drunk?"
Baozhu clutched Xi Rongyan and nodded rapidly.
Then, head bowed low in desperate appeal: "It is entirely this servant's fault for leading the young miss astray. I beg Your Majesty's forgiveness."
Wei Qi gave a low hum of acknowledgment. "Go and call Madam Xi to come take the Fourth Young Miss home."
Baozhu hesitated. "But the young miss, alone here..."
The words were barely out before she felt a piercing, ice-cold gaze settle on her.
She could not explain the sensation — no sound had come, yet her whole body went cold with sudden dread.
She understood, belatedly: the Emperor's authority was absolute. How could anyone dare to question him?
She had spoken out of turn. Heart hammering, she pressed her forehead to the floor and agreed.
Telling herself that the Emperor was here — nothing would go wrong.
Trembling, she then coaxed Xi Rongyan in a soft voice, afraid her young mistress would cause a scene: "Miss, I am going to fetch the qin for you. Wait here a moment — I'll be right back."
Xi Rongyan's world was already a haze. She only knew she was burning inside, unaware of where she was, dimly hearing Baozhu's voice.
The fingers clutching Baozhu's sleeve loosened a fraction. One pale hand pressed against the floor. A few strands of dark hair fell across her brow, and she urged in a slurred murmur: "Hurry..."
Baozhu did not dare delay. Seeing her mistress somewhat settled, she scrambled to her feet and ran to fetch the lady of the house.
Taking a few steps, she turned back to cast an uneasy glance at the young miss still on the floor, thought that she had better bring Madam here as quickly as possible, steeled herself, and turned away.
She dashed outside and looked up on instinct at the sign above the door — and nearly stopped breathing. This was not Qingshan Pavilion at all. It was Qingyue Pavilion.
But where was Qingshan Pavilion?
She looked to the side — and her heart lurched again. Qingshan Pavilion was the building right next door.
But she had clearly looked just now and it had said Qingshan Pavilion.
There was no point in puzzling over it now. With a sense of cold despair, she slapped herself on the forehead, knowing she had made a terrible mistake, and ran as fast as she could to find the lady of the house.
Inside the room, the moment Baozhu was gone, Chief Gao tactfully withdrew to the window outside. He glanced after Baozhu's panicked retreating figure, made a brief gesture, and a guard slipped silently in pursuit.
In the room, Xi Rongyan, half-dazed on the floor, her thoughts floating in and out like clouds, was calling out again to go and see the flowers. She looked up at the black figure before her and reached out one slender hand, latching straight onto Wei Qi's robe.
Wei Qi had only loosely draped the crane robe over himself. Xi Rongyan's tug sent it sliding half off, baring his broad, solidly muscled chest. The robe pooled over Xi Rongyan's hand, and she stared at it in confused bewilderment, still lost.
Wei Qi lowered his eyes and looked at Xi Rongyan — her dark brows framing unfocused, fog-drifting eyes. In silence, he bent and gathered her up into his arms.
He held her on his lap, his knuckled fingers tracing, inch by inch, from her soft waist to her back, letting the figure in his arms nestle and shift against him.
He bowed his head and pressed a kiss to the top of her hair, breathing in the familiar warmth of her scent. His black eyes were fathomless.
Xi Rongyan's pale fingers curled around the wide cuff of his sleeve. In a voice like a murmuring cat, she whispered: "The peach blossoms are out... I want to pick some and make peach blossom tea..."
A sound like the soft mewing of a cat. Wei Qi cast his eyes down again and watched Xi Rongyan. His fingers caught her chin. In those eyes, he was not reflected at all.
His thumb, with its heavy ring, passed over her shimmering, misted gaze — the rosy flush deepening, her dark brows clear and still. He pressed his lips together, the shadows in his eyes deepening.
Only in moments like this would she draw close to him of her own accord.
His fingers tightened involuntarily — and only when the figure beneath them made a small restless sound did he ease his grip. He drew her closer, patting her back: "You like peach blossoms. I will have every palace hall planted with them."
"You will have peach blossom tea to drink every year."
Xi Rongyan seemed not to hear him at all. Her fingers crept up to his throat, and then she suddenly lifted her misty eyes and burst into a soft, bright laugh — as though she were playing with her beloved cat.
A sweet fragrance reached him. Wei Qi looked at the eyes turned up to him — shimmering with fog, curved with laughter, warm with the scent of the Hundred Flower Wine.
He rarely saw Xi Rongyan smile. She had never once smiled at him.
She was always so frightened of him.
Always finding ways to escape him.
He leaned slowly forward, his black eyes blazing with an almost unbearable intensity, watching her smile: "Yan'er."
Xi Rongyan heard him. She gave a vague, unknowing hum of reply, and then her fingers wandered up to press against the face before her.
She tilted her head slightly to look into the eyes in front of her — somehow deeply, strangely familiar.
She looped her arms around his neck. Her fine brows half-lowered. The jade pin in her dark hair slipped free and fell with a clear, ringing crack against the floor. In the aftermath of that sound, she murmured very softly: "I have seen you in my dreams."
Wei Qi's black eyes shifted. He gazed into Xi Rongyan's eyes, his hand tightening at her waist. In a low, slow voice, he asked: "What did you dream of me?"
Xi Rongyan pouted. As though looking upward had tired her, she buried her face against Wei Qi's neck, her voice small and aggrieved: "You bully me."
"Always bullying me..."
Wei Qi pressed his lips together. The long fingers at Xi Rongyan's waist tightened another degree.
If only she had been a little more yielding, he would not have felt the need to keep her so confined.
She had fled so many times before. He had punished her for it — so why did she still keep trying to leave?
The figure in his arms was still restless, her fingers now wandering into the opening of his robe, drifting lower. Wei Qi drew a measured breath and caught her hand.
Xi Rongyan felt stifled — she wanted to climb off Wei Qi and go pick peach blossoms.
Wei Qi held her and soothed her: "Wait a moment. I will have someone pick you a whole basket."
Xi Rongyan, eyes shut, insisted on pulling Wei Qi along, and yet she could not so much as stand upright — her body limp as spring water.
Wei Qi, afraid she would hurt herself, reached to hold her — and was promptly toppled onto his back beneath her.
Her warmth and fragrance pressed close against him. He looked up at her dazed, fluttering eyes, watched the red lips part: "So hot..."
He could no longer hold back what his body wanted. He reached up and kissed her lips.
Breathless, he whispered between kisses: "Yan'er. Who am I?"
Xi Rongyan only gave soft, muddled cries, her unfocused eyes making it abundantly clear to Wei Qi that the figure in his arms did not know who he was.
Wei Qi's eyes darkened another shade. He held her and bore her down onto the daybed, and his punishment of a kiss pressed over her lips.
Xi Rongyan only felt her lips being bruised with a dull ache. Tears shimmered at the corners of her eyes. Dazed, she laid her hand on Wei Qi's broad back.

chapters.title: An Imperial Decree
chapters.content:
On one side, Lady Xie had been deep in promising conversation with the Xuanyi Marquisate — learning that the Marquisate was indeed interested in the match, which delighted her enormously.
She was thinking that her daughter's marriage might soon be settled, when Chunyun came rushing up and bent close to Lady Xie's ear to whisper a single sentence.
Lady Xie's expression changed at once. She quickly rose and drew Chunyun aside to ask, "What did you say? The young miss is not in Qingshan Pavilion?"
Chunyun nodded urgently. "I brought the sobering tea and searched all of Qingshan Pavilion for a long while without finding the young miss. Then I came straight back."
Lady Xie, knowing how little Xi Rongyan was aware of herself when in drink, felt a knot of alarm in her chest. She pressed urgently: "And have you seen Baozhu?"
Chunyun shook her head quickly. "No, not her either."
Lady Xie, afraid that something had gone wrong, quickly excused herself to the Marchioness and hurried with her maidservants toward Qingshan Pavilion.
On arrival, there was truly no one.
Lady Xie knew Baozhu was steady and capable — if something were truly amiss, there must be a reason.
She could not say what made her do it, but she turned to look — and caught sight of Qingyue Pavilion not far away.
Could they have taken the wrong path and gone into Qingyue Pavilion?
With that thought she made for the neighboring hall at once.
The moment she stepped inside, she heard a sound.
A familiar sound — her own daughter's voice.
She quickened her steps and followed the sound. The first thing her eyes fell upon was a daybed with its curtain drawn down, and clothing on the floor — no one's but Xi Rongyan's.
And from behind the curtain, a thin, hoarse voice: "Don't go..."
Lady Xie's heart gave a terrible lurch. Her gaze then found, on the floor, a pair of man's black boots — embroidered with dragons.
The world went black before her eyes. She nearly fainted where she stood.
She immediately waved all the maidservants behind her out of the room.
She was about to speak when the curtain was lifted by a long, elegant hand, and the Emperor emerged — cold-faced, his gold-dragon crane-robe gathered around him — and sat upright. A smear of Xi Rongyan's lip rouge was visible on his cheek.
And Xi Rongyan, wearing only her inner robe, clung to Wei Qi's waist. One pale shoulder was half bared; beneath the thin white robe, the suggestion of the bodice beneath was visible. She was murmuring for the Emperor to play the qin, entirely unaware of what she was doing.
Lady Xie's vision swam again. Her legs gave way beneath her, and she sank in a panicked kowtow.
She had not thought — she could never have imagined — to witness this.
Lady Xie struggled through waves of dizziness and said with difficulty: "This subject's daughter has today misbehaved under the influence of wine and offended Your Majesty. I beg Your Majesty's forgiveness."
"This subject will take her daughter away at once and deal with her properly."
Wei Qi sat at his ease on the edge of the daybed, one hand still resting at Xi Rongyan's waist.
He looked at the woman kneeling before him, his voice cool and unreadable: "I had come here to take some peace and quiet today — it was indeed disturbed."
"But bearing in mind that the Fourth Young Miss was not herself due to wine, I will let this pass."
"However, as she has already been seen by me, and there has been contact between us, given that things have reached this point, I shall, for the sake of the Fourth Young Miss's honor, receive her into the palace in two days' time."
As he spoke, Wei Qi was already drawing Xi Rongyan's garments into order. He spoke then in a tone that left no room for refusal: "The decree will be issued in due course. You need only await it."
Lady Xie felt the world tilt again.
The inner palace was a place of intricate hearts and machinations — far more treacherous than the fighting among women in an ordinary household. How could her daughter be a match for those women?
And yet, with things having come to this point, the Emperor himself had spoken so plainly.
Furthermore, what she had just witnessed...
She felt sick at heart. The match with the Xuanyi Marquisate had been almost settled, and now this had happened.
She had not yet thought through how to accept it, when from above came the Emperor's suddenly cold and forbidding voice: "Or does Madam Xi object to her entering my inner palace?"
Lady Xie, pressed by the Emperor's authority, knew the weight of the imperial will — and no grounds on which to refuse it. The Emperor had made himself clear, and her daughter sat now in his arms in just such a state. Whether she wished it or not, she had no argument.
Besides, she could not know what had already passed between Rongyan and the Emperor. If...
The bewildered woman could only steel herself to comply: "It is Rongyan's fortune to be able to serve Your Majesty in the palace. This subject is also grateful that Your Majesty does not hold Rongyan's improper conduct against her."
The cold edge of Wei Qi's expression softened slightly. He dismissed Lady Xie.
Lady Xie drifted out in a daze, then sagged against the nanny at her side — and for a long while could not come back to herself.
Xi Rongyan, who had been sitting in Wei Qi's arms, had by this point spent most of her energy and was now drifting toward sleep, leaning against Wei Qi's shoulder.
Her hair had long since come loose, falling over her pale shoulders. She lay quietly against him.
Wei Qi held her for a long while, then eased her down onto the daybed and rose.
When Wei Qi stepped out, he was fully and properly dressed, his bright yellow dragon robe in perfect order. He stood before Lady Xie, his towering figure bent slightly to look down at the woman with her head bowed before him. His expression was the cold, inscrutable authority of a ruler.
He clasped his hands behind his back. His voice was light: "Madam Xi, make your preparations. I will issue the decree today. The day after tomorrow, the Fourth Young Miss will be received into the palace."
He walked past her without another word.
Only when the Emperor's retreating figure had vanished did Lady Xie finally come back to herself — she had even forgotten to offer her thanks.
She hurried into the room. Behind the bed curtain, Xi Rongyan lay sleeping with her clothing all in order, completely unaware of anything that had happened.
